doc.title: Jackie McLean — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Playing for Bud, Richard Powell and Bob Bunyan
summary: Bud has McLean play Buzzy, McLean gets Richard Powell started and sends him to the older pianist Bob Bunyan.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: But it’s obvious what you had in the case.

Yeah, a saxophone. Yeah, I’m scared. He said, “Take it out. Can you play it?” I was like, “I know Buzzy,” because I knew that one song. So he said, “Buzzy? What’s Buzzy?” So I took it out, and I played [McLean sings the opening phrase], and he started playing. That was it. He was impressed, because I was playing – by this time I was playing two years and had been practicing and had been trying to play anything of Bird’s that I could or anything of Pres’s, Dexter. So he liked the idea that I was so young and that excited about the music. So he – his mother was very nice to me. Me and Richard became tight. I started Richard playing, because he wouldn’t let Richard play the piano. Bud wouldn’t teach him anything and told him, “No, you can’t play the piano.” Richard was younger than me, even, by maybe a year-and-a-half, two years. So I got Richard started playing. I said, “Man, you don’t have to wait for Bud. I know somebody that plays just like Bud that will show you.”
A guy named Bob Bunyan, a piano player that lived in Harlem. So I took Richard to Bob, and Bob started teaching him.
Bob Bunyan’s a name that comes up, I guess, in A. B.’s text [A. B. Spellman]. You probably mentioned him. Tell us about him and what happened to him.
I don’t know what happened to Bob. I just knew that he was much older than me. He was about Bud’s age and played good.
Yeah. Played good, and it was through going around to jam sessions and things that I met him and heard him play and played with him. But I was real young compared to many of those guys.
